description: NEXPLORA is a creative team that turns imagination into interactive experiences. Through our project, we create a virtual lunar mission where users can explore the Moon, build their own base, manage resources, and experience the challenges of living beyond Earth through an engaging, game-like simulation.
summary: NEXPLORA is a browser-based 3D lunar survival game for kids (ages 7–12) that teaches real NASA engineering trade-offs. Over a 10-day mission, players balance Power, Life Support, and Radiation Shielding where "No Choice Is Free." Driven by real NASA data (DONKI, OSDR, VIPER), every decision creates cascading consequences, turning passive learners into critical-thinking space commanders with zero downloads required.
details:
NEXPLORA: LUNAR OUTPOST is a 3D browser game for kids aged 7 to 12. The player is an astronaut sent to the Moon to build a base from scratch. There is nothing to download and no account to create. A child opens the page, picks a landing site, and starts exploring.

Most space content for kids is either a poster full of facts or a game with little real science in it. Kids rarely see what mission planners actually deal with: you can’t have everything. If you spend power on one thing, you may run short on another. I wanted a game where every choice costs something, so kids learn this idea by playing.

The mission lasts ten in-game days, and each day has its own goal. The child first chooses one of three landing sites: Shackleton Crater Rim, Cabeus Crater Floor, or South Pole Ridge. Each site changes the mission, for example how much sunlight there is for solar power or how hard the terrain is.

After landing, the child walks the astronaut around with the keyboard or mouse, moves the camera, and collects food, water, oxygen supplies, building materials and science samples. These are used to build a habitat, solar panels, a life support unit, a storage station, a radiation shelter, a science lab and a rover bay. Buildings are placed in the 3D world with a preview, and their cost is taken from the inventory.

Built units then have to be turned on and managed. Life support uses power. A stronger radiation shelter uses materials that could have gone into solar panels. Sending the rover out explores more of the Moon but costs energy. Nothing is free, and the game explains why a number dropped and how to fix it.

Commander Nova is the guide who stays with the player. She reacts to what is really happening: what the child is standing next to, what they hover over, or what is missing from the inventory. Every object and button also has a tooltip that explains what it is and why astronauts need it.

I wanted the science to be real, so the game uses NASA open data. Space weather events from DONKI drive the solar activity alerts, so a real solar flare or coronal mass ejection decides how serious a storm is and whether the radiation shelter matters that day. Radiation dose values from the OSDR RadLab database give a real baseline for the radiation mechanic, and OSDR research provides short facts about how spaceflight affects the human body. The in-game NASA Science Center shows real NASA images with sources and credits. Food facts come from the Canadian Space Agency’s toolkit on growing food on the Moon. If a live source is unavailable, the game switches to saved real data and labels it as saved, not live.

After ten days, the child has a working base, a mission rating, badges, and an Explorer Passport that records what they built and discovered. Most importantly, they see that survival in space means balancing power, air, water, food and protection, and that every decision has a consequence.

React, TypeScript, Vite, Three.js with React Three Fiber, and Tailwind CSS. Progress is saved in the browser, so kids can continue later.
